passages.t: The pool, and a man ill for thirty-eight years
passages.happening:
Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for a feast. John does not say which one.

Near the Sheep Gate there is a pool called Bethesda, with five covered walkways around it (verse 2). On these walkways lie many sick people: the blind, the lame, the paralyzed. One man there has been ill for thirty-eight years (verse 5).

Jesus sees him and knows he has been there a long time. He asks him, “Do you want to get well?” (verse 6). The man does not say yes. He explains why he is still lying there. “Sir,” he says, “I have no one to help me into the pool when the water is stirred. While I am on my way, someone else goes in before me” (verse 7).

Jesus does not discuss the pool. He says, “Get up, pick up your mat, and walk” (verse 8). At once the man is well. He picks up his mat and walks. Then John adds the line that starts all the trouble: “Now this happened on the Sabbath day” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
For a long time some readers thought John's ‘five covered colonnades’ were made up, perhaps a picture of the five books of Moses. Then digging near the Church of St Anne in Jerusalem, north of the old temple area, uncovered two large pools separated by a rock wall. Walkways on the four sides and one across the middle wall would give five. Many scholars now take this as the pool John describes, though some details are still debated. It is a small sign that the writer knew Jerusalem before the Romans destroyed it in AD 70.

In later Roman times there was a healing shrine at this place to Asclepius, the Greek god of healing; it belongs to the city the emperor Hadrian rebuilt after AD 135. Whether people already came there for that god in Jesus' day is not certain. But verse 7 shows that the sick believed the stirred water could heal, and that the first one in had the best hope.

So picture the scene. A crowd of sick people, each watching the water, each hoping to be first. And one man who has no one, and so is never first.
passages.ot:
The man's thirty-eight years may remind a Jewish reader of Israel in the wilderness. Moses said, “The time we spent traveling from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed over the Brook of Zered was thirty-eight years” (Deuteronomy 2:14). That echo is possible, but John does not point to it.

What the prophets did promise is clear. Isaiah saw a day when “the lame will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6). A man who has not walked for nearly four decades walks away carrying his bed. To John's readers, that is a sign that the day the prophets spoke of has begun.
passages.hard:
Two questions here. First, what about verse 4? If you look at this chapter in the Berean Standard Bible, verse 4 is missing; the number is skipped. Older Bibles such as the King James Version print it. It says that an angel came down at certain times and stirred the water, and the first person in after that was healed. The oldest copies of John do not have it: the early papyri P66 and P75, from around AD 200, and the great fourth-century books Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus all go straight from verse 3 to verse 5. Most scholars think a scribe added it later, probably to explain why the man in verse 7 talks about the stirring of the water. That is why most modern Bibles leave it out or put it in a note. Nothing in Christian teaching rests on this verse. And the story does not need the angel. John's point is that the man is healed without the pool at all.

Second, is ‘Do you want to get well?’ a rebuke, as if the man secretly wanted to stay ill? Some preachers have read it that way. But the man's answer is not an excuse. It is a lament: no one helps him. And Jesus asks for no right answer and no faith before he heals him. The question is not blame. It is the first time in years that anyone has spoken to him about his life.
passages.asks: Some people have waited a very long time for help that never came. If that is you, notice who Jesus chose. Not the quickest, not the one with friends, but the man left behind. And notice that Jesus did not tell him to try harder to reach the water. He came to him where he lay. If you live with a long illness or disability, this story does not say you lack faith or desire. It says you have not been overlooked.

passages.t: The Sabbath, and making himself equal with God
passages.happening:
Some of the leaders see the man carrying his mat. “This is the Sabbath,” they tell him. “It is unlawful for you to carry your mat” (verse 10). He answers that the man who healed him told him to. But he does not know who it was; Jesus has slipped away into the crowd.

Later Jesus finds him at the temple and says, “See, you have been made well. Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you” (verse 14). The man goes and tells the leaders that it was Jesus.

Now they begin to persecute Jesus for doing such things on the Sabbath. Jesus answers, “To this very day My Father is at His work, and I too am working” (verse 17). That makes it worse. “Because of this, the Jews tried all the harder to kill Him. Not only was He breaking the Sabbath, but He was even calling God His own Father, making Himself equal with God” (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
A word about ‘the Jews’ in this chapter. Here, as often in John, the phrase means the religious authorities in Jerusalem, the leaders around the temple, not the Jewish people. Jesus is Jewish. The healed man is Jewish. The crowds at the pool are Jewish. These verses were later misused to blame a whole people, and that misuse is wrong. John's book page explains this in its part on ‘the Jews’ in John.

Why did carrying a mat matter? The Sabbath, the seventh day of rest, was one of the great marks of Jewish life. The commandment forbade work but did not list every kind of work, so teachers worked it out. Carrying a load was named already by the prophets. The Mishnah, a book of Jewish teaching written down around AD 200, lists thirty-nine main kinds of forbidden work, and the last is carrying something from one place to another (Shabbat 7:2). It is later than Jesus, but it shows how seriously carrying was taken. To the leaders, a man walking through the city with his bed was breaking the Sabbath in plain sight.

Jesus' answer in verse 17 built on something Jews already believed. God rested on the seventh day, yet he never stops keeping the world alive. Philo, a Jewish thinker in Alexandria in Jesus' own time, wrote that God never stops making things, as it is the nature of fire to burn (Allegorical Interpretation 1.5). So when Jesus said, ‘My Father is working, and I am working’, his hearers understood him. He was claiming to do what only God does, on God's own day. That is why John says he was ‘making Himself equal with God’.
passages.ot: The Sabbath was rooted in creation: “by the seventh day God had finished the work He had been doing; so on that day He rested from all His work” (Genesis 2:2). The commandment said, “Remember the Sabbath day by keeping it holy” (Exodus 20:8). And Jeremiah had named carrying: “do not carry a load or bring it through the gates of Jerusalem on the Sabbath day” (Jeremiah 17:21). The leaders were not inventing a rule. They were defending something God had given. The question Jesus raises is who is Lord of that day, and what God's own work on it looks like.
passages.hard:
Does ‘Stop sinning, or something worse may happen to you’ (verse 14) mean that the man's illness was a punishment for his sin? It does not say so. Jesus does not say what caused the thirty-eight years. He warns the man that sin leads to something worse than lameness. In chapter 9 the disciples ask about a man born blind, “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he was born blind?” Jesus answers, “Neither this man nor his parents sinned, but this happened so that the works of God would be displayed in him” (9:2-3). In Luke he refuses to say that people who died in a disaster were worse sinners than others (Luke 13:2-3). So John does not teach that illness is always punishment, and no one should use this verse to tell a sick person that their sickness is their fault.

And does Jesus really claim to be equal with God, or is that only what his enemies thought? John states it as his own explanation in verse 18, and he does not correct it. The rest of the chapter, as the next notes show, goes on to give the Son what belongs to God alone.
passages.asks: The leaders saw a man carrying a mat and missed a man who could walk. It is possible to be so sure about the rules of God that we miss the work of God in front of us. And it is possible, like this man, to receive great help from Jesus and not yet know who he is. He went looking for the man again. He does that still.

passages.t: The Son does what the Father does
passages.happening:
Jesus answers the charge, and he does not take back a word. “Truly, truly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing by Himself, unless He sees the Father doing it. For whatever the Father does, the Son also does” (verse 19). The Father loves the Son and shows him everything he does.

Then Jesus names two things that only God does. First, giving life: “just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom He wishes” (verse 21). Second, judging: the Father has given all judgment to the Son, “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father” (verse 23).

And then the promise: “whoever hears My word and believes Him who sent Me has eternal life and will not come under judgment. Indeed, he has crossed over from death to life” (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Jesus' hearers would picture a family trade. In that world a son learned his father's work by watching him at the bench. He did what he saw his father do. Jesus uses that picture for himself and God.

They would also know a principle of Jewish law, written down later in the Mishnah, that a man's agent is like the man himself (Berakhot 5:5). To dishonour a man's messenger is to dishonour the one who sent him. Jesus says the same in verse 23.

But Jesus says more than an agent could. He gives life ‘to whom He wishes’. He will judge all people. He is to be honoured ‘just as’ the Father is. No messenger, prophet or angel was ever given that.
passages.ot: In the Old Testament, giving life and judging the world belong to God alone. God says, “I bring death and I give life” (Deuteronomy 32:39). Hannah sang, “The LORD brings death and gives life; He brings down to Sheol and raises up” (1 Samuel 2:6). And God will not share his glory: “I will not yield My glory to another” (Isaiah 42:8). When Jesus claims both works and the same honour, he is placing himself on God's side of that line.
passages.hard:
If the Son ‘can do nothing by Himself’, is he less than God? This question is very old. In the fourth century a teacher named Arius pointed to verses like 19, 26 and 30 and said the Son was the first and greatest thing God made, but not God in the same way as the Father. Some groups today read the chapter in a similar way.

The church answered at the councils of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381). Its teachers pointed to the same chapter. The Son does whatever the Father does (verse 19). He gives life to whom he wishes (verse 21). He judges all (verse 22). He is honoured just as the Father is (verse 23). He has life in himself (verse 26). No creature can do these things. So the words about the Son depending on the Father describe the way the Son relates to his Father, and his obedience as a man, not a lower kind of being. The Nicene Creed, in the older English wording printed on this site, confesses him as ‘very God of very God, begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father’. This is what the creeds bind all Christians to confess.
passages.asks: Verse 24 is one of the plainest promises in the Bible. Whoever hears and believes has eternal life now, and has already crossed over from death to life. If you fear that you are still on the wrong side of that line, read it again slowly. It does not say ‘whoever has earned it’. It says whoever hears and believes.

passages.happening:
Jesus goes on. “The hour is coming and has now come when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live” (verse 25). The Father has life in himself, and he has given the Son to have life in himself too (verse 26). And he has given him authority to judge, because he is the Son of Man (verse 27).

Then Jesus looks further ahead. “The hour is coming when all who are in their graves will hear His voice and come out” (verses 28-29). Those who have done good will rise to life; those who have done evil will rise to judgment.

He ends where he began: “I can do nothing by Myself; I judge only as I hear. And My judgment is just, because I do not seek My own will, but the will of Him who sent Me” (verse 30).
passages.hearers:
John's Gospel holds two times together. Some things are true now: the hour ‘has now come’, and people who hear Jesus begin to live, even before they die. Other things are still to come: the day when the graves open. Scholars sometimes call these the ‘now’ and the ‘not yet’. John keeps both. Eternal life starts today, and the resurrection of the body is still ahead.

‘Son of Man’ was Jesus' favourite way of speaking about himself. Hearers who knew the book of Daniel would remember a figure ‘like a son of man’ who comes with the clouds and is given authority by God. That is the background for verse 27: the Son of Man is the one given authority to judge.
passages.ot: Daniel saw the day these verses describe: “many who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake, some to everlasting life, but others to shame and everlasting contempt” (Daniel 12:2). Ezekiel heard God say, “I will open your graves and bring you up from them” (Ezekiel 37:12). Jesus claims that it is his own voice that will call the dead out.
passages.hard: Does verse 29 teach that people are saved by doing good? ‘Those who have done good’ will rise to life. Read alone, that could sound like salvation by good works. But John's Gospel explains its own words. In the next chapter, when people ask what work God wants, Jesus says, “The work of God is this: to believe in the One He has sent” (6:29). And in chapter 3, people who do what is true come to the light (3:21). In John, the good deeds of verse 29 grow from coming to Jesus; they are not a way around him. Christians in different traditions explain how faith and works fit together in different ways, but none of them reads this verse as a way to be saved without Christ.
passages.asks: Jesus will judge the world, and his judgment is just, because he seeks his Father's will and not his own. That is good news for everyone who has been judged unfairly. The last word on your life will not be spoken by people who did not know you, or who judged you for their own ends. It will be spoken by one who is just.

passages.happening:
Now Jesus speaks like a man in court. “If I testify about Myself, My testimony is not valid” (verse 31). So he calls other witnesses.

The first is John the Baptist. The leaders sent to him, and he told the truth. “John was a lamp that burned and gave light, and you were willing for a season to bask in his light” (verse 35).

The second is Jesus' own works: “the very works I am doing” show that the Father sent him (verse 36). The third is the Father himself (verse 37). The fourth is the Scriptures: “You pore over the Scriptures because you presume that by them you possess eternal life. These are the very words that testify about Me, yet you refuse to come to Me to have life” (verses 39-40).
passages.hearers:
Jewish law did not convict anyone on the word of one witness. Two or three were needed. Jesus grants that a man speaking only for himself is not enough (verse 31), and then goes beyond it. He calls four witnesses.

His hearers loved the Scriptures. As verse 39 says, they searched them for eternal life, and these men knew them far better than most. Jesus does not mock that. He says they were right to look there for life, and that the Scriptures point to the one standing in front of them.

The lamp in verse 35 is a fine picture of John the Baptist. He was a lamp, not the light; John's Gospel said that on its first page (1:8). Lamps burn themselves out. John did, in Herod's prison.
passages.ot: The Law itself required more than one witness: “A matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Deuteronomy 19:15). And when Jesus says the leaders have never ‘seen His form’, he echoes Moses at Sinai: “You heard the sound of the words, but saw no form; there was only a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12). Even Moses was told, “no one can see Me and live” (Exodus 33:20). The Father whom no one has seen has now borne witness in his Son.
passages.hard: Does verse 39 mean that Bible study is useless, or that we can skip the Scriptures and go straight to Jesus? No. Jesus calls the Scriptures one of his witnesses. He does not tell anyone to stop reading them. He says that reading them without coming to him misses their point. Later the risen Jesus will explain to two disciples ‘what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself’ (Luke 24:27). The Bible and Jesus are not rivals. The Scriptures lead to him, and he opens the Scriptures.
passages.asks: It is possible to know the Bible well and still not come to the one it speaks about. That is a warning for anyone who reads much, preaches often, or studies hard, and it is a warning for these notes too. The point of reading is not only to know more. It is to come to him and have life.

passages.happening:
Jesus ends with the hardest words of the chapter. He does not want praise from people (verse 41). But he says to his opponents, “I know you, that you do not have the love of God within you” (verse 42). He came in his Father's name and they did not receive him; someone who comes in his own name, they will receive.

Why can they not believe? “How can you believe if you accept glory from one another, yet do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?” (verse 44).

And then the surprise. Jesus will not accuse them before the Father. “Your accuser is Moses, in whom you have put your hope. If you had believed Moses, you would believe Me, because he wrote about Me” (verses 45-46).
passages.hearers:
Moses was Israel's great defender. When God was angry with the people after the golden calf, Moses pleaded for them (Exodus 32:11). Jesus' hearers trusted that Moses was on their side. So it would shock them to hear Moses called their accuser. Jesus is not attacking Moses. He is claiming Moses as a witness on his own side.

Verse 44 names something every religious community knows. People want the good opinion of the people around them. They wait to see what the respected men think before they decide. Jesus says that makes faith impossible. A person who needs the approval of the room cannot follow someone the room has rejected.
passages.ot: Where did Moses write about Jesus? Christians have pointed to several places. The promise of a prophet like Moses: “The LORD your God will raise up for you a prophet like me from among your brothers. You must listen to him” (Deuteronomy 18:15). The snake lifted up in the wilderness, which Jesus has already used (3:14; Numbers 21:8-9). The Passover lamb. And the manna, which the next chapter takes up. Philip said it in chapter 1: “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law” (1:45). Moses also placed the Book of the Law beside the ark “as a witness against you” (Deuteronomy 31:26), which is just what Jesus says it has become.
passages.hard: Were these words said to all Jewish people? No. They were said to particular leaders in Jerusalem who were seeking to kill Jesus (verse 18). Jesus himself, his disciples, and the healed man were all Jewish, and Jesus appeals to Moses and the Scriptures as true witnesses, not as a rival faith. Christians who later turned these verses against Jewish people misread them badly. The warning in verse 44 is for every religious person, and that includes Christians: we too can prefer each other's praise to God's.
passages.asks: Ask yourself whose approval you are really waiting for. Many people do not reject Jesus because of an argument. They hold back because of what the people around them would think. Jesus says the glory that comes from the only God is worth more than all of it.
